section_1.title: Prerequisite Review: Vectors and Areas
section_1.content: Define a vector as a directed line segment in 3D space. Introduce the concept of a 2D parallelogram spanned by two vectors, u and v, as the foundation for the cross product.
section_1.example: Imagine two robotic arms of lengths |u| and |v| emerging from the origin; the area they enclose represents the magnitude of their interaction.

section_2.title: Defining the Cross Product: Direction and Magnitude
section_2.content: Explain that the cross product u × v produces a new vector perpendicular to the plane formed by u and v. Its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram, and its direction is determined by the Right-Hand Rule.
section_2.example: Use a 3D animation showing a right hand curling from vector u to v, with the thumb pointing in the direction of the resulting vector w.

section_3.title: Geometric Intuition: Orientation and Volume
section_3.content: Introduce the scalar triple product (u × v) · w, which geometrically calculates the signed volume of the parallelepiped defined by three vectors. This links the cross product to the concept of spatial orientation.
section_3.example: Visualize a 'container' box formed by three edges; as one vector changes direction, show the volume 'flipping' from positive to negative as the orientation changes.

section_4.title: The Linear Transformation Perspective
section_4.content: Explain that the cross product u × v can be viewed as a linear transformation. Specifically, the operation (u ×) is a skew-symmetric matrix transformation that maps any vector w to a vector perpendicular to both u and w.
section_4.example: Show a 3D grid 'twisting' under the influence of the skew-symmetric matrix, illustrating how it rotates and scales vectors simultaneously.

section_5.title: Summary and Real-World Application
section_5.content: Summarize how cross products bridge geometry (areas/volumes) and linear algebra (determinants/transformations). Conclude with a practical application in physics/graphics.
section_5.example: A game engine calculating surface normals: Using the cross product of two edges of a polygon to determine which way a character's face is pointing for proper lighting calculation.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 1.5 + j * 0.8
                y = 2.0 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        u = Vector([2, 0.5, 0], color=BLUE)
